title: Would you rather face the coldest day ever recorded on Earth, or the hottest?
lines: Colder than dry ice, or [134 °F](a hundred and thirty-four degrees)?
Would you rather face Earth's coldest day ever, or its hottest?
Pick one right now, and comment A or B. Think fast.
Option A: Vostok Station, Antarctica, [July 1983](July, nineteen eighty-three).
[Minus 89.2 °C](Minus eighty-nine point two Celsius). Colder than dry ice.
In July, the Sun never rises there.
At that cold, exposed skin can freeze in minutes.
Satellites later spotted hollows on the ice sheet near [minus 98 °C](minus ninety-eight).
Option B: Death Valley, California, [July 1913](July, nineteen thirteen).
[134 °F](A hundred thirty-four Fahrenheit), the hottest ever officially recorded.
Thirty degrees hotter than a hot tub's safety limit.
In [1972](nineteen seventy-two), the ground hit [201 °F](two hundred and one degrees).
Rangers say drink a gallon of water a day.
So which one wins? By the science, the hot day.
With shade and water, crowds visit every summer.
Without polar gear, Vostok's cold would beat you far faster.
At the South Pole, the [300 Club](three hundred club) tries both.
They sit in a [200 °F](two hundred degree) sauna, then run outside at [minus 100 °F](minus one hundred).
A three hundred degree swing. So which would you pick?
